chunks.text: concepts and actually do the programming? So what are some topics we'll be covering? We will be, at the core of it, learning computational thinking. So in the future, when you encounter a problem, your first thought shouldn't be how do I kind of mathematically

chunks.text: to answer the question, how do we know the programs we write are efficient? We can write programs, but how do we know that they're fast and how do we know that they don't take up all the memory in the computer?

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: OK. So let's start by talking about knowledge. Declarative knowledge is a statement of fact, and a lot of us, probably in math and in the past, have worked with declarative knowledge.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: But this is not how computer science, this is not how this class works. In computer science, what we do is we work with imperative knowledge, which is basically a recipe, how to do something.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: And when we're programming, all we're doing is writing a recipe for the computer to do something. That's it. So here's a numerical example. The first statement is a declarative statement.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: The square root of a number x is y, such that y times y is equal to x. There are many possible values for x and y that this statement can be true. But if we gave that statement to a computer,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: it wouldn't know what to do with it. What we need to do is tell the computer how to find the square root of a number, and then tell us what the square root of that number is. And so the computer then needs a recipe.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So the recipe, a really simple one for finding the square root of a number, is steps 1, 2, 3. So what we do is let's say we want to find the square root of 16. We obviously know it's 4, but the computer doesn't. And so we give it an initial guess.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: Let's say the guess is 3. How do we go from there? So the steps we follow, step 1, if 3 times 3, 9 is close enough to 16, we can stop. It's not really close enough for me.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So let's keep going. Step 2, otherwise, so we're going to make a new guess by averaging g, which is our original guess 3, and x over g, which is 16 over 3. 16 was the square root we wanted to find.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So our next guess is 4.17. OK, using the new guess, repeat the process until we are close enough. So we go back to step 1. That's the first part of the process.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: We find guess squared. 4.17 squared is 17.36. So now we say, is that close enough? Not really. It's 17.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: It's not really even close to 16. So let's do it again. We make a new guess by averaging 4.17 and 16 divided by 4.17. That gives us our new guess 4.0035.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: Next step, using the new guess, we repeat the process. So 4.0035 squared is 16.277, 0.277. Is that close enough to x? Yeah, I could be happy with this.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: I could stop there because we're within plus minus 1. So I'm OK with that. But if we wanted to be within plus or minus 1 times 10 to the negative, like 6 or 7 or something like that, then we would continue the process.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So really what we had there is an algorithm. It's a sequence of steps, step one, step two, step three. There's some sort of flow of control. We had a place where we said, if the guess is close enough, then we can stop.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: Otherwise, we do something else. We had another flow of control where we said, repeat this thing. So we're not going linearly, but we're changing the flow. And then lastly is a way to stop.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: We don't want the algorithm to go on forever. We would like to stop at some point. And the stopping point, I was kind of vague about it. But it could be when we were within plus or minus 1 of the actual answer.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: And so recipes are basically algorithms. My grandmother was basically teaching algorithms when she would teach me to bake a cake. She didn't call it that, but she was, really. And so even recipes have that same structure.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: There's a sequence of steps. There's a flow of control, like if you don't have egg, use egg substitute. Or repeat this, you know, repeat sticking a toothpick to see if it comes out clean every minute,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: or something like that. And then there's a way to stop, right? When the toothpick comes out clean, you take it out of the oven and you eat it. And so computers are machines that

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: execute these algorithms. They're actually dumb, right? Computers are not very smart. They don't make decisions on their own. They just follow these sequences of steps

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: that we told them to do. Computers are good at storing lots and lots of data, right? We can't really do that. But computers can store gigabytes of storage, terabytes even, and computers can do operations really, really

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: quickly, which is something we can't do, right? They're good at those two things, but they're not very smart. They can't make decisions unless they're told to make the decisions. So really, the computer only does what you tell it to do.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: And that's one of the big ideas that I want you to come away from this lecture with. The computer only does what you tell it to do, right? The sequences of steps that you tell it to do, that's the only thing it follows.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So a little brief history just to kind of make you appreciate Python programming language before we actually get started with it is, you know, before the 1940s, we had these things called fixed program computers, like a pocket calculator is an example of that.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: Every button was an operation. In the little screen, you could use parentheses to put a bunch of different operations together, but there was no way to sort of store all these operations together to later put in different inputs

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: for that same sequence of operations. You had to input it every single input, those sequences of operations. After the 1940s, stored programs computers came into play, and they were able to store instructions to do things as data.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: And there was a special program called an interpreter that executed these instructions. It knew how to follow simple sequences of steps when the program told it to go to a different location. So it was a special program called an interpreter

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: that executed these instructions. It told it to go to a different location it did. So it was basically executing these instructions. And the instructions that it did were arithmetic and logical, so addition, subtraction, things like that.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: Simple tests, like checking for equality between two values and moving data, so taking this value and putting it at a different memory location. So I just wanted to give you a really brief overview, and this is not super accurate, but it

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: gives you a sense of how exactly things happen low level in the computer. So the computer basically has memory, where things are stored. It has an arithmetic logic unit that does operations. It knows how to add things, subtract things, multiply things,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: compare things. And then it has the control unit, where this program counter is set. And this is where you put a program in. So let's see if this works.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: This is a program. And up here is our memory. So we have a bunch of memory locations, 3, 4, 5, 6, 3, 4, 5, 7. And at each of these memory locations,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: we have some values stored, prefilled. So when we first run this program, what ends up happening is the interpreter sees the first instruction, add the values at 3, 4, 5, 6, and 3, 4, 5, 7 together. So it goes to these memory locations here,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: grabs the 3 and the 4, and sends them to the arithmetic logic unit. The ALU knows how to do the addition. So it adds 3 plus 4, 7, and sends the result back here. Now, we never told it to store that result anywhere,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: but the next instruction says store the value you just got back from the ALU at this memory location, 3, 4, 5, 8. So the next step basically takes that 7 and stores it at memory location 3, 4, 5, 8. Super tedious.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: All we did was add 3 plus 4. We do that again. We add the values at 7, 8, 8, 9, and 7, 8, 9, 0. So it goes in the memory, it grabs the 5 and the 2, sends it to the ALU.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: The ALU calculates it as 7, brings it back, and then we store that in location 7, 8, 9, 1. And then after that, all we've done is two additions. And then the next instruction says compare the values at memory locations 3, 4, 5, 8,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: and 7, 8, 9, 1. So we're going to compare the 7 with the 7. The ALU, again, does this comparison and says, all right, well, 7 and 7 are equivalent. So this is true or whatever it wants to give back

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: to the interpreter. And then the last instruction here we have is print the result of that comparison. So we print true because they were equal. Again, super high level, but it kind of

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: gives you an appreciation for programming languages these days, right? This is very tedious to write if we had to write programs in this manner. Alan Turing a long time ago showed

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: that you can compute anything with actually a very even more basic set of primitives, not addition, subtraction. But instead, with a tape, you would actually have six primitives. Move the tape left, move the tape right,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: read the value at the tape, put a value on the tape, erase the value from the tape, and no operation. And so since he showed this, what the result of it actually was is down here. Anything computable in one language

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: is computable in any other programming language. So if we had some program written in Java, that basically boils down to something super long, but something that is made up of these six primitives, that means that if we boil down this program

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: to these six primitives, we can build back up the same program in a completely different language. And that's really powerful. That's a really cool statement. Now, we're not going to be working with those primitives.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: We're going to be using the Python primitives, which are more convenient, and they allow us to do a lot more things in much less time. I'm going to do a little comparison as we talk about the primitives of Python with English.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So in English, some of the primitives might be words, or even we can do letters or characters, but we can say it's words. With characters, we can build up words. With words, we can build up sentences.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: With sentences, we can build up stories. With stories, we can build up books and things like that. In programming languages, the primitives are numbers, sequences of characters, operators like addition, multiplication, division, checking for equality,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: checking that something is greater than, things like that. So once we have these primitives in a language, we can start to build up the syntax of the language. So in English, having something like noun, and noun, and noun doesn't make any sense, right?

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: Catdog boy doesn't make much sense. It's not syntactically valid. But noun, verb noun, is syntactically valid, right? Similarly, in programming languages, we can have two objects kind of side by side.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So here, this is a sequence of characters h and i, and this is the number 5 right beside that sequence of characters. But that doesn't make any sense, right? What does it mean to have this sequence of characters and that number right beside it?

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: It has no meaning in Python. Instead, what we have to do is we have to add an operator in between these two objects. So here, we add a little star operator in between the sequence of characters high and the number

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: 5. And in Python, the meaning to this is I want to repeat the sequence of characters high, h, i, five times. So this would basically give me high, high, high, high, high.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So once we have sentences in English and expressions that are syntactically valid, we can now talk about the static semantics of the language. So in English, saying something like, I are hungry is syntactically correct,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: but it's not static. It's not, sorry, it doesn't have good static semantics. There's no meaning to that, because the R is for you or plural. Similarly, in programming languages,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: and this will differ depending on what programming language you use, here, in the previous slide, we saw that you can use the star operator between the sequence of characters and the number. And that meant repeat that sequence many times.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: But if we use a plus operator in between the sequence of characters and a number, that doesn't have any meaning in Python. So it has a static semantic error, even though it's syntactically valid.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: We have object operator object. So so far, we've been able to find really nice parallels with English, the English language in the programming languages, but this is kind of where things break down. When we talk about the semantics of a language.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So in English, you can have many different meanings. The chicken is ready to eat means let's eat this chicken, or the chicken is ready to eat means the chicken wants to eat something. Programming languages, there is no multiple meanings

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: to a program that you write. Because the computer, the machine, the language, follows the set of instructions to a T, there is no ambiguity about what it needs to do. It just follows the instructions and does what it needs

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: to do to the end, till it terminates the program. And so programs only have one meaning, but the problem is it might not be the meaning that you intended it to have. And that's when things start to go wrong.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: We can have syntactic errors in our program, spelling errors, indentation errors, things like that. And those are easy to catch. Static semantic errors are 90% probably easy to catch. But the problem comes in with the semantics, right?

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: The meaning that you intended this program to have might not be what it's actually doing. And that's where most of my errors happen. And that's where I get super frustrated when I program. And that's probably where you guys

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: will get super frustrated, too. Because you write a program that you think is doing one thing. But instead, either it crashes right away or it runs forever and doesn't really stop. Or it terminates, but it gives you an incorrect answer.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: It's not what you were expecting. And we'll talk about this in a few lectures. So when we write programs, we're basically writing sequences of definitions and commands. And we're going to write these either in a file editor

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: or in a shell. The first today, at least, we're writing in the shell directly. And half of tomorrow, we'll write in the shell. Because we're not really writing many lines of code. I'm just going to be showing you some really quick things

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: that we can do with the Python programming language. So hopefully, you all have installed the programming environment. This is the code editor. So tomorrow, we'll start working in here.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: But for today, we're really just going to work in the shell. And even in the future, you can still type commands in the shell. I find the shell very useful if there's just something really quick that I want to check that I don't want to write a program for and then run.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: It's just like a simple command that I want to check to make sure it's doing what I think it's doing before I insert it in my code editor. So here, we have this. So mine is, I guess, I'm using the white theme

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: just because I find it easier for you guys to see. This is the file editor. And this is just a bunch of expressions or a bunch of code that we're going to type in today. And we're going to type it in the shell today.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So the thing on the right-hand side. OK, so what exactly do we do when we write a program? At the base of it, we are going to create objects inside our programs. And we're going to manipulate them. That's it.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: That's what programming is mostly about at its core. Now, when we create objects, it's important. This is kind of something we're going to come back to again and again in a kind of more high-level setting. But right now, what I want you to understand

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: is that when we create an object, an object has a type. And the type that an object has tells Python the things you're allowed to do with that object. So here are two examples. The number 30, it's a number.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: The type, we'll talk about it in a bit. The type is an integer. It's a whole number. But basically, what are the things we can do with this integer, with this number?

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: We can add it to another number. We can subtract it to another number. We can take it to another power. We can take some other number to this power of 30. A bunch of sort of mathematical operations, as you would expect.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So that's pretty straightforward. What about this one here? This quotation, capital A lowercase n, lowercase a quotation. So this is something we'll talk about next lecture. It's called a string.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: And it's a sequence of characters. The quotations tell Python it's a sequence of characters. And the characters, part of it are capital A, lowercase n, lowercase a. The kinds of things I can do with this string

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: are not the same kinds of things I'm allowed to do with a number. If I tried to take Anna and divide it by the sequence of characters Bob, Python would complain very much.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: Because you can't divide a string by another string. A sequence of characters doesn't make sense to divide it by another sequence of characters. Similarly, I can't take Anna to some power. I can't multiply by itself, things like that.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: But the kinds of things that I am allowed to do on a sequence of characters is different than the kinds of things I'm allowed to do on a number. So the things I can do with a sequence of characters

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: is I can say, well, what's the character at the first position? What's the middle character? How long is the sequence of characters? How many characters do I have? And so now you can see that the type of the object

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: is actually really important. Python uses it to know the kinds of operations you're allowed to do with it. And so there's actually scalar objects. And these are Python's primitives, numbers, and truth values.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: And there are non-scalar objects. We're not talking about these yet. We'll talk about these in a few lectures. But these have some sort of structure. So for example, a list of numbers

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: has a structure because there's a number at the beginning of the list, there's a number at the end of the list, things like that. But a number itself doesn't have a structure. It's just the number.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So what are the types of the scalar objects? What are the types of the primitives in Python? Integers, so number 5, 0, negative 100, a million. Float is another type. It represents all the real numbers, so 3.27.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: 2.0 is a float because it has a decimal number, even though to us that just means 2. But to Python, if you put in 2.0, it says that's a type float. Negative 3.14159, things like that.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: Bull is a boolean. It represents truth values. And there's only two possible values that a boolean type has, true and false. And it has to be capital T true and capital F false.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: And the last one is this non-type type. It's literally called non-type. And it has only one special value, none. We're not going to talk about it for a bit, but we will sometime in the future.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So to figure out the type of an object when you create that object, you use the type command. So we can say something like type, parentheses. And this is a command. And inside the parentheses, you say,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: what do you want to find the type of? So if we do type of 7, it tells me it's an int. And if you want to do the same command again, I hit the up arrow. And it automatically puts in what I wrote previously.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: And then if I want to do type of 0.0, it's a float, because there's a decimal point. So this is basically what I said. So we type this in the shell. And the shell tells us what the output is.

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: So just to reiterate, int, float, bool, and non-type are types of objects. And there can be many different objects you can create of that type. So if you think about it, ints and floats,

chunks.title: Introduction_To_CS_and_Programming
chunks.text: we basically have an infinite number of objects we can create of those types, because we can have 0, 1, 2, 3, 100, 200, 300, a million. And all the negatives. There's almost an infinite number of values, objects,
